General Guidelines

Assignment objective¶

The aim of the assignment is to implement a document (sentence) classification model with (standard) machine learning methods. The assignment in total has 30 points; it also offers 2 extra points which can cover any missing point.

This Notebook encompasses all aspects of the assignment including the descriptions of tasks as well as your solutions and reports. Feel free to add any required cell for solutions. The cells can contain code, reports, charts, tables, or any other material, required for the assignment. Feel free to provide the solutions in an interactive and visual way!

Please discuss any unclear point in the assignment in the provided forum available in MOODLE. It is also recommended to provide answers to your peer's questions. However when submitting a post, keep in mind to avoid providing solutions. Please let the tutor(s) know shall you find any error or unclarity in the assignment.

Libraries & Dataset¶

The assignment should be implemented with recent versions of Python (>3.7). Any standard Python library can be used, so far that the library is free and can be simply installed using pip or conda. Examples of potentially useful libraries are scikit-learn, numpy, scipy, gensim, nltk, spaCy, and AllenNLP. Use the latest stable version of each library.

To conduct the experiments, we use a subset of the HumSet dataset [1] (https://blog.thedeep.io/humset/). HumSet is created by the DEEP (https://www.thedeep.io) project – an open source platform which aims to facilitate processing of textual data for international humanitarian response organizations. The platform enables the classification of text excerpts, extracted from news and reports into a set of domain specific classes. The provided dataset contains the classes (labels) referring to the humanitarian sectors like agriculture, health, and protection. The dataset contains an overall number of 17,301 data points.

Download the dataset from the Moodle page of the course.

the provided zip file consists of the following files:

  • thedeep.subset.train.txt: Train set in csv format with three fields: sentence_id, text, and label.
  • thedeep.subset.validation.txt: Validation set in csv format with three fields: sentence_id, text, and label.
  • thedeep.subset.test.txt: Test set in csv format with three fields: sentence_id, text, and label.
  • thedeep.subset.labels.txt: Captions of the labels.
  • thedeep.ToU.txt: Terms of use of the dataset.

[1] HumSet: Dataset of Multilingual Information Extraction and Classification for Humanitarian Crises Response Selim Fekih, Nicolo' Tamagnone, Benjamin Minixhofer, Ranjan Shrestha, Ximena Contla, Ewan Oglethorpe and Navid Rekabsaz. In Findings of the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (Findings of EMNLP), December 2022.

Task A: Pre-processing & Feature Extraction (15 points)

Preprocessing (5 points). Load the train, validation, and test sets. Study the text and according to your judgements, apply at least two text cleaning/preprocessing methods. Punctuations marks, numbers, dates, case-sensitivity are some examples of the elements which can be potentially considered for cleaning/preprocessing. Tokenize the result text with a tokenizer of your choice. Report your approaches to text cleaning and tokenization and the reasons of your choices. Provide some examples, showing the effects of the applied approaches on the text.

Creating dictionary (5 points). Create a dictionary of vocabularies following the guidelines discussed in the lecture. Next, reduce the size of dictionary using a method of your choice, for instance by considering a cut-off threshold on the tokens with low frequencies. When removing tokens from the dictionary, consider a strategy for handling Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) tokens, namely the ones in the train/validation/test datasets that that are not anymore in the dictionary. Some possible strategies could be to remove OOVs completely from the texts, or to replace them with a special token like <OOV>. Explain your approaches and report the statistics of the dictionary before and after the reduction.

Creating sentence vectors (5 points). Use the dictionary to prepare two variations of document representation vectors, separately for train, validation, and test sets. Both variations follow a Bag-of-Words approach with a different token weighting method. One applied weighting must be tf-idf and the other one can be any other method discussed in the lecture such as tc, tf, BM25. These term weighting methods should be implemented; using a library to readily calculate the term weightings is not allowed. Report the applied approaches. Calculate and report the sparsity rate of the vectors of train, validation, and test sets, namely what percentages of the vectors in each set are filled with zeros.

Preprocessing:¶

This one of the most important steps of any NLP task. After inspecting the data files, there are no instances of URLs for example which should be accounted for. There were many quotes, some instances of capitalised words such as "for OVER 2 weeks" with [OVER instead of over] (test_data id = 10707). There were many instances of "numbers". There were also instances of multiple white spaces eg. id = 14982 and id = 10037 in train_data.

(1) Text normalization:

  • For text normalization we first but everything to "lower".
  • There were many numbers in the text which maybe could be indicative of a label so those where also harmonised them to ".".
  • Then punctuations were removed which are considered irrelevant for further processing.
  • The occurences of multiple white spaces have also been removed.
  • Stop words have been removed, which are the most frequent words in a document and carry no semantic meaning. So those were removed.

(3) Tokenization: For Tokenization lemmatization was used to reduce variation and inflections to their base forms. Although lemmatization might not work for "new words" as they have no equivalent in the dictionary, lemmatization was used as it does not harm precision and does not increase ambiguity unlike stemming.

In [ ]:
lemmatizer = WordNetLemmatizer()
stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english'))

def prep_data(text):
    text = text.lower()
    text = re.sub(r'(\d+)[,.](\d+)', r'\1<decimal>\2', text)
    text = re.sub(r'[^a-z0-9\s<>]', '', text)
    text = text.replace('<decimal>', '.') # convert all , to . 
    tokens = word_tokenize(text)
    tokens = [word for word in tokens if word not in stop_words]
    tokens = [lemmatizer.lemmatize(word) for word in tokens]
    return tokens

train_data['cleaned_tokens'] = train_data['text'].apply(prep_data)
test_data['cleaned_tokens'] = test_data['text'].apply(prep_data)
validation_data['cleaned_tokens'] = validation_data['text'].apply(prep_data)

Creating the dictionary¶

Replacing tokens that are not in the entire dictionary with the OOV token¶

In [7]:
train_tokens = sum(train_data["cleaned_tokens"], [])
vocab_freq = FreqDist(train_tokens)
thold = 10
reduced_vocab = {word: freq for word, freq in vocab_freq.items() if freq >= thold}
reduced_vocab["<OOV>"] = 0

def compute_oov(tokens, vocab):
    return [token if token in vocab else "<OOV>" for token in tokens]

train_data["processed_tokens"] = train_data["cleaned_tokens"].apply(lambda x: compute_oov(x, reduced_vocab))
validation_data["processed_tokens"] = validation_data["cleaned_tokens"].apply(lambda x: compute_oov(x, reduced_vocab))
test_data["processed_tokens"] = test_data["cleaned_tokens"].apply(lambda x: compute_oov(x, reduced_vocab))

Tokens which are less frequent than 10 (threshold = 10) were replaced with the OOV token. We did not remove them but replace those tokesn to prvent loss of information. Because some labels of text might have more OOVs. The threshold was set to 10 (after several tryouts on different threhold values) to still have some variety in the vocab size as can be seen below the original vocab size was 33899 and reduced to 5136 after setting the threshold to 10 (see all statistics blow).

Term frequency (version 2)¶

$$x_{v,d} = tf_{v,d} = \log(1 + tc_{v,d})$$

Inverse document frequency¶

$$idf_v = \log\left(\frac{M}{df_v + 1}\right)$$

Term frequency-Inverse document frequency¶

$$\log(1 + tc_{v,d}) \times \log\left(\frac{M}{df_v + 1}\right)$$
In [9]:
#tf
def compute_tf(tokens):
    tc_vd = Counter(tokens)
    for term in tc_vd:
        tc_vd[term] = log(1+tc_vd[term])
    return tc_vd

#idf
def compute_idf(num_docs, vocab):
    M = len(num_docs)
    idf = {}
    for word in vocab:
        df_v = sum(1 for doc in num_docs if word in doc)
        idf[word] = log(M / (df_v+1)) 
    return idf

#tf-idf
def compute_tfidf(tokens, idf):
    tc_vd = compute_tf(tokens)
    tfidf = {term: tc_vd[term] * idf[term] for term in tc_vd}
    return tfidf

Sparsity rates¶

In [18]:
vocab = reduced_vocab.keys()

def compute_sparsity(vects, vocab_size):
    sparsity = []
    for vect in vects:
        zeros = sum(1 for term in vocab if term not in vect)
        sparsity_perc = (zeros/vocab_size)*100
        sparsity.append(sparsity_perc)
    return sparsity

train_tfidf_sp = np.mean(compute_sparsity(train_tfidf, len(vocab)))
validation_tfidf_sp = np.mean(compute_sparsity(validation_tfidf, len(vocab)))
test_tfidf_sp = np.mean(compute_sparsity(test_tfidf, len(vocab)))

print(f"tf-idf sparsity | train: {train_tfidf_sp}")
print(f"tf-idf sparsity | validation: {validation_tfidf_sp}")
print(f"tf-idf sparsity | test: {test_tfidf_sp}")

tf-idf sparsity | train: 99.35868730561752
tf-idf sparsity | validation: 99.36756434533838
tf-idf sparsity | test: 99.37318801433382

The tf-idf sparsity as can be seen above is arround 99.35-99.37% in across all three sets.

Task B: Training and Results Analysis (15 points)

To evaluate the models, use accuracy as the metric.

Dummy baseline (2 points). Create one dummy baseline classifier that predicts the validation/test labels only based on the distribution of the labels in the training set (without any use of the feature vectors). This is a weak baseline and acts as a sanity check for the actual classifiers.

Training and tuning classifiers (5 points). Select at least two classification algorithms from standard machine learning classifiers. Using each classification algorithm, train a machine learning model on each of the variations of feature vectors. This should result in four experiment sets (2 variations of feature vectors × 2 classification algorithms). The ML model in each of the experiments possibly have several involving hyper-parameters. For each experiment, select one of the hyper-parameters and tune its value. The tuning process is done by first assigning at least three values to the hyper-parameter, then training separate models based on each value, and finally using the evaluation results on the validation set to select the best-performing model. Report the studied hyper-parameters, the evaluation results of each on validation set, and finally the selected value of the hyper-parameter.

Evaluation, reporting results, and discussion (3 point). Evaluate the selected models of the four experiments on the test set. Report the results of the four experiments on both validation and test sets (side by side) in one table as well as in one plot. Compare different experiments and models. Are the test results lower(/higher) than the validation results? If it is the case, where can it be rooted from? Among all these models and variations, what are the most important factors improving the classification results?

Confusion matrix (2 point). Select the best performing model among the experiments and use it to create a confusion matrix. The matrix shows the predicted versus true results per each label. Explain your observations on the matrix. Across which classes do you observe significant confusions?

Features visualization (3 point). Continue with the best performing model and now take its feature vectors for the dataitems in the test set. Project these feature vectors to a 2-dimensional space using the TSNE method. Using these 2-dimensional vectors, create two plots where the dataitems are shown as points (small circles) on the plots. The plots look exactly the same but only differ in the coloring of the data points. The first plot colors every dataitem with its true label, while the second one colors each according to its predicted label by the model. Keep in mind to assign the same colors to the classes of the plots, so that the plots are visually comparable. Put these two plots side by side, observe the differences, and compare the results. Report your observations.

dummy_clf = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent")

validation_preds = dummy_clf.predict(validation_data['text'])

test_acc = dummy_clf.score(test_data['text'], test_data['label'])
val_acc = dummy_clf.score(validation_data['text'], validation_data['label'])

In [35]:
C_values = [1, 5, 10]

Training and Tuning classifiers¶

For the experiments TF and TF-IDF were chosen as well as logistic regression and svc. Logistic regression (LR) has the advantage that it can be trained quite fast but the disadvantage is that it might underperform when the classes can't be seperated linearly. SVC, on the other hand, can be used to find complex decision boundaries, but can be computationaly expansive.

Experiment #1 | Running SVC on tf-idf with C={1,5,10} as regularization params (VALIDATED ON VALIDATION SET)¶

In [42]:
#using the tf-idf from sklearn
vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words='english')
X_train_tfidf = vectorizer.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_tfidf = vectorizer.transform(X_test)
X_validation_tfidf = vectorizer.transform(X_validation)

for C in C_values:
    print(f"training on tf-idf | SVC with C={C} | validated on validation set")
    svc_model = SVC(C=C, 
                    kernel=kernel, 
                    degree=degree, 
                    gamma=gamma, 
                    coef0=coef0,
                    tol=tol,
                    decision_function_shape=decision_function_shape)

    svc_model.fit(X_train_tfidf, y_train)
    y_pred_validation = svc_model.predict(X_validation_tfidf)
    print(f"Classification report | C={C}")
    print(classification_report(y_validation, y_pred_validation))
    print("\n")

Evaluation, reporting results, and discussion¶

All models performed much better than our dummy baseline.

For the selected values of C in both tf and tf-idf, the accuracy always stays around 80%, therefore we decided to use the metrics form tf-idf, for the results on tf validation and test see above.

Accuracy on the test set (SVC) tf-idf¶

\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Model} & \textbf{Accuracy} \\ \hline \text{SVC (C=1)} & 0.79 \\ \text{SVC (C=5)} & 0.80 \\ \text{SVC (C=10)} & 0.80 \\ \hline \end{array}

Accuracy on the validation set (SVC) tf-idf¶

\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Model} & \textbf{Accuracy} \\ \hline \text{SVC (C=1)} & 0.79 \\ \text{SVC (C=5)} & 0.80 \\ \text{SVC (C=10)} & 0.80 \\ \hline \end{array}

Accuracy on the test set (Logistic Regression) tf-idf¶

\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Model} & \textbf{Accuracy} \\ \hline \text{LR (C=1)} & 0.80 \\ \text{LR (C=5)} & 0.79 \\ \text{LR (C=10)} & 0.79 \\ \hline \end{array}

Accuracy on the validation set (Logistic Regression) tf-idf¶

\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Model} & \textbf{Accuracy} \\ \hline \text{LR (C=1)} & 0.80 \\ \text{LR (C=5)} & 0.81 \\ \text{LR (C=10)} & 0.81 \\ \hline \end{array}
In [132]:
models = ['SVC (C=1)', 'SVC (C=5)', 'SVC (C=10)', 'LR (C=1)', 'LR (C=5)', 'LR (C=10)']
test_accuracies = [0.79, 0.8, 0.8, 0.8, 0.79, 0.79]
validation_accuracies = [0.79, 0.8, 0.8, 0.8, 0.81, 0.81]

bar_width = 0.35
index = np.arange(len(models))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))

bar1 = ax.bar(index, test_accuracies, bar_width, label='Test Set', color='skyblue')
bar2 = ax.bar(index + bar_width, validation_accuracies, bar_width, label='Validation Set')

ax.set_xlabel('Model', fontsize=14)
ax.set_ylabel('Accuracy', fontsize=14)
ax.set_title('Model Accuracy Comparison: Test vs Validation Set', fontsize=16)
ax.set_xticks(index + bar_width / 2)
ax.set_xticklabels(models, rotation=45, ha='right', fontsize=12)
ax.legend(loc='lower right')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

For the LR validation set accuracy was higher for C=5 and C=10 which could indicate overfitting. For all other instances the test and validation set accuracy was the same which could indicate the model is neither overfitting nor underfitting.

In [ ]:
#Best performing model
lr_model = LogisticRegression(C=10, max_iter=1000)
lr_model.fit(X_train_tfidf, y_train)
y_pred_validation = lr_model.predict(X_validation_tfidf)
cm = confusion_matrix(y_validation, y_pred_validation)
In [90]:
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
plt.imshow(cm, interpolation='nearest', cmap=plt.cm.Blues)
plt.title('Confusion Matrix for LR (C=10) | Validation Set', fontsize=16)
plt.colorbar()
plt.xlabel('Predicted Labels', fontsize=14)
plt.ylabel('True Labels', fontsize=14)

labels = [str(i) for i in range(12)]
plt.xticks(np.arange(12), labels, rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=12)
plt.yticks(np.arange(12), labels, fontsize=12)

th = cm.max() / 2.
for i in range(12):
    for j in range(12):
        plt.text(j, i, format(cm[i, j], 'd'),
                 ha="center", va="center", color="white" if cm[i, j] > th else "black", fontsize=12)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

TP (true positive) was well for class 4 (health), 9 (protection) and 10 (shelter), 11 (WASH). For label 0 there were many FP (false positive) estimates more than FN (false negative). Class 6 and 7 were also very badly predicted. Class 0 (agriculture) shows a notable confusion with class 5 (livelihood). Class 1 (cross) shows notable confusion with class 9 (protection) and 10 (shelter). Class 6 shows notable confsion with class 9. Class 7 (NFI) also shows notable confusion with class 9 (protection). The confusion between agriculture and livelihood would be easy to argument cause there could be an overlap in vocabulary, as well as for all other confused labels.

Task C: Linear Model Interpretability (2 extra points)

Train a logistic regression model on one of the document representations. Take the coefficient weights, learned by the model, on each dimension (which here corresponds to each token in the dictionary). Separately for each class, study what are the tokens that have the highest contributions/importance for the predictions of the model.
In [137]:
reduced_vocab = {word.lower(): freq for word, freq in reduced_vocab.items()}
tf_idf_vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(vocabulary=reduced_vocab.keys(), lowercase=True)

train = tf_idf_vectorizer.fit_transform(train_data['text'])

label_encoder = LabelEncoder()

y_train = label_encoder.fit_transform(train_data['label'])
y_validation = label_encoder.transform(validation_data['label'])
y_test = label_encoder.transform(test_data['label'])

lr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=100000)
lr.fit(train, y_train)

feats = tf_idf_vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()
coefs = lr.coef_
In [141]:
top_tokens = 20
tokens = {}

for index, class_label in enumerate(label_encoder.classes_):
    sorted_indices = coefs[index].argsort()
    top_pos = sorted_indices[-top_tokens:]
    top_neg = sorted_indices[:top_tokens]

    tokens[class_label] = {"positive_tokens": [(feats[i], coefs[index][i]) for i in top_pos],
                           "negative_tokens": [(feats[i], coefs[index][i]) for i in top_neg]}

for class_label, tokens in tokens.items():
    print(f"\nClass: {class_label}")
    print("#" * 40)
    print("Top 20 positive tokens")
    positive_tokens = {token: f"{weight:.4f}" for token, weight in tokens["positive_tokens"]}
    pprint(positive_tokens)
    print("\nTop 20 negative tokens")
    negative_tokens = {token: f"{weight:.4f}" for token, weight in tokens["negative_tokens"]}
    pprint(negative_tokens)
    print("#" * 40)
